title: Exactly what happens if we run out of water?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with news on the collapsing Darfur peace accord and the Sudanese government's bombing of SLM-held villages, tying Darfur's conflict to access to drinking water. They discuss global water scarcity (about 1.2 billion people without clean water, child deaths from unsafe water), the US average of 158 gallons per day versus about 12 gallons needed for survival, and water as a cause of conflict (a World Bank vice president's warning about future wars over water, and a Georgia–Tennessee–Alabama–Florida border dispute over the Tennessee River). They walk through the cascade from water shortage to crop failure, farmer migration to cities, and infrastructure breakdown. They cover glaciers that supply billions of people and are melting, desalination as expensive, bioengineered drought-tolerant crops, agriculture using about 70% of water with inefficient irrigation, drip irrigation, and carrying capacity (hunter-gatherer era versus agriculture). A sponsor read for Visa and a recipe segment for a frozen-fruit breakfast smoothie with vanilla protein powder close the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and Darfur peace accord news
segments.summary: Hosts open the show and discuss the collapse of the Sudanese government's peace accord with a rebel faction after the army bombed villages under SLM control, and the possible indictment of President al-Bashir.

segments.title: Water access and the Darfur conflict
segments.summary: Discussion that the Darfur conflict began partly over access to drinking water, and that about 1.2 billion people lack clean drinking water, with about 6,000 children dying each year from unsafe water.

segments.title: Water use and survival needs
segments.summary: Hosts note that a person needs about 12 gallons of water a day, while Americans average about 158 gallons a day, and that water is cheap and undervalued.

segments.title: Water as a cause of conflict and border disputes
segments.summary: A World Bank vice president's warning that future wars would be fought over water is discussed, along with a Georgia dispute with Tennessee, Alabama and Florida over the Tennessee River border, and the difference between neighboring states and hostile nations.

segments.title: The cascade effect of running out of water
segments.summary: Hosts explain that people can survive about 60 days without food but only 3 to 5 days without water, and that water shortage leads to crop failure, farmer migration to cities, infrastructure strain and pollution.

segments.title: Glaciers, desalination, and irrigation
segments.summary: Discussion of melting glaciers that supply billions with water, why salt water can't be drunk, expensive desalination plants, bioengineered drought-tolerant crops, and agriculture using about 70 percent of water with inefficient irrigation; drip irrigation is mentioned as a solution.

segments.title: Carrying capacity
segments.summary: Chuck explains carrying capacity as the maximum population a resource base can sustain, contrasting hunter-gatherer populations with the larger population enabled by agriculture, and the hope that technology will keep ahead of limits.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Josh closes with a remark about drinking his out-of-date Fresca, and the hosts wrap up the topic.
